newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rosy EU forecasts likely to meet market scepticism.
newsitem.headline: Rosy EU forecasts likely to meet market scepticism.

text.p: Economic forecasts to be issued by the European Commission next week are expected to show key EU countries making the grade for the single currency -- a prediction which markets are likely to greet with scepticism.

Economists said any hint by the Commission on November 6 that Germany and France would not meet the Maastricht treaty criterion of a budget deficit at or below three percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1997 could cause a sharp market reaction.

The reason is not that markets believe the two countries to be on track to meet the necessary criteria. It is that the Commission, despite attempts to be unbiased, is considered an advocate of the European Union's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Not painting a rosy picture would be seen as a sign that the project was in trouble.

"The problem is that if it comes out with a figure that is higher than three percent for the deficit, it is going to get itself into a lot of trouble," Holger Schmeiding, senior economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt, said.
"(But) if it comes out with a figure of three percent or less, people are not going to believe it," he said.
Eric Chaney, senior economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris, agreed. "What would surprise the markets is to see one of the actors in the process saying...Germany and France cannot reach three percent.
"This would be proof that something is really wrong," he said.

Both said the Commission, which produces economic forecasts twice a year, was seen by the markets as an interested party. "It is not an independent analyst looking at Europe from the moon," Chaney said.

The Commission rejects such charges, arguing that its statistical staff are as professional and as unbiased as those found in other multinational organisations such as the International Monetary Fund.
"Our forecasts are prepared with the highest standards of objectivity and transparency on our methods," a spokesman for Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said.
The last time the Commission issued its forecasts, in May, France and Germany were said to be on track for the single currency, defying market expectations.
This time, recovery in Germany is expected to help the Commission continue with a bullish forecast for the single currency.
"The Commission's spring forecasts seem to be broadly confirmed for Europe as a whole, in particular the pickup of growth in the second half of 1996," de Silguy's spokesman quoted him as saying.

"We have always believed there would be a significant number of countries able to meet the necessary conditions to participate in monetary union from 1 January 1999. I would say today that this number is probably increasing," he continued.
A number of questions, however, still remain for the Commission as it puts the final touches to the report.
One is whether a planned transfer of 37.5 billion francs ($7.3 billion) from France Telecom to French government finances could be counted as lowering the country's public deficit.
A decision is expected next week.

Another is how to reflect Italy's planned austerity programme in its calculations. In May, the Commission included a 50 billion mark ($33 billion) German savings plan in its forecasts even though it had not at the time been approved by parliament. ($1=5.113 French Franc) ($1=1.5130 Mark)
